Hello world!
I dont know whether I should create a separate channel for this or just a topic in this channel... I am formalizing the theory of set coloring games in Lean4! the study of set coloring games through the lens of combinatorial game theory is fairly new, starting with Peter Selinger's paper "On the combinatorial value of Hex positions" published in Intergers in 2021. So far I would like to formalize this paper, along with my masters thesis on Reverse Hex.

Here is my GitHub page. A lot of my code is based on the combinatorial-games library, with adjustments made where necessary.

Here is Peter Selinger's original paper, and here is my masters thesis.
I will try to update here when I have problems with my code, when I have learned something about implementation, and maybe keep a to-do list.

Here is a list of what i have so far:

  • A datatype that represents (a precursor to) set coloring games over a set of outcomes via QPFs
  • API that allows us to not think about QPFs (for the most part, still working on that)
  • ofSets notation (not as an instance, need to fix this)
  • well-founded relation Subposition
  • well-founded induction
  • definition of addition with HAdd instance (addition is heterogeneous)
  • definition of MAP, a way to get from a game over set A to a game over set B via a function f:A->B.
  • definition of Dual, the conjugate (or negation) of a set coloring game
  • some theorems proved

What remains to be done:

  • My ofSets is not an instance of the typeclass defined in the CGT library
  • My tactic Primordial_wf should be optimized, it is currently a bit silly.
  • Set coloring games should contain a pair of non-empty sets of games, so I must make a subtype of Primordial A that reflects this.
  • definition of outcome classes for games over Bool
  • definition of contextual order
  • probably other stuff I cannot remember currently

I have just pushed a large update to the git repository.

I noticed that, if recursive functions (sum, MAP, Dual, etc.) are defined using { st } rather than { s | t } proofs become much easier. this is because the definitions of these things are pretty much the same regardless of player (i.e., the definition for the right set is usually the same as the definition for the left set, except roles are reversed). I feel that this is why games are defined as being functions from Player to sets of games in the first place.

Something funky happened with my tactic Primordial_wf after I changed the definitions to all my recursive functions. Before the change, the tactic would to solve all the decreasing_by goals immediately. Now, I have to write something like decreasing_by all_goals {cases p <;> Primordial_wf}. I could just add cases p to the tactic, but i feel there is a less intense way to fix this (it is not good to generate a lot of cases if you do not have to).
I was sucessfully able to rework my ofSets to instead be an instance of the ofSets described in the CGT library
just pushed the change mentioned above.

successfully fixed primordial_wf. I did this in a suboptimal way: I created a new lemma

lemma Subposition.of_mem_movesP {A : Type} {x y : Primordial A} {p : Player} (h : x ∈ (moves.{u} y) p) : Subposition x y := by
  suffices x∈ ⋃ p, (moves.{u} y) p by exact Subposition.of_mem_moves this
  · rw [Set.mem_iUnion]
    use p

That is almost identical to a previous theorem:

theorem Subposition.of_mem_moves {A : Type} {x y : Primordial A} (h : x ∈ ⋃ p, (moves.{u} y) p) : Subposition x y :=
  Relation.TransGen.single (h)

I feel there is a better way of doing this...
just pushed some changes. defined strategies, outcome classes, and proved the fundamental theorem of CGT.

Pushed a new change in which I defined the intrinsic order on games. I was able to use a cool technique that i learned about here. This was necessary in the definition of intRel.leq and the proof of transitivity. Essentially, it remembers the order in which you proved things recursively. Go check it out, it's cool!
Sorry for not reading this yet, I'll check this out in about a week or so. I need to finish my thesis and I won't be online very much till then.

I have just pushed a few updates. I proved that g≤h  ⟺  hop≤gopg \leq h\iff h^{\text{op}}\leq g^{\text{op}}g≤h⟺hop≤gop (these are the theorems leq_Dual and tri_Dual). This is similar to the idea that g≤h  ⟺  −h≤−gg\leq h \iff -h\leq -gg≤h⟺−h≤−g in normal play games. Unfortunately I have to be a bit more careful with types. I also wrote two proofs, left_sub and right_sub. These statements and proofs are naturally dual, so I tried to prove right_sub "by duality" after proving left_sub. There were definitely places where I could have done better, but I don't know how exactly yet. It would be nice to write a tactic that tries to prove things "by duality": if A and B are dual theorems, It applies leq_dual and tri_dual to everything, then tries to prove theorem B using theorem A (refer to the proof of right_sub for a better example of this...).

@Violeta Hernández I made a notation for the op of a game (this is similar to the negation or the conjugate of a game.) It is in the file Hex.lean, just look up op. I want to use theorems about the function Dual when referring to op. Currently op g is an abbreviation of @Dual Aᵒᵈ g. When I use my op notation, I have to rewrite all occurrences of op. This is sub-optimal. Is there a nice way to get around this?
you could make it a notation

@Aaron Liu I currently have the following:

noncomputable abbrev op {A : Type} [Preorder A] (g : Primordial A) := @Dual Aᵒᵈ g
notation g:max "ᵒᵖ" => op g

I first tried to just write notation g:max "ᵒᵖ" => @Dual Aᵒᵈ g but this did not work. The Aᵒᵈ is important, it tells lean to take the preorder on A and reverse it. I am not sure if there is a way around this. I do not want to supply the type A and its instance of a preorder, that defeats the purpose of the shortcut :(

If I can't figure something out I may just create lemmas for op that are the same as the lemmas for dual, which would save me from needing to rewrite it all the time.

Oh I should include the definition of Dual:

noncomputable def Dual {A : Type} (x : Primordial A) : Primordial A :=
if IsAtom x then
  x
else
  !{fun p=>Set.range (fun (z : x.moves (-p)) ↦ Dual z)}
termination_by x
decreasing_by
  Primordial_wf

As you can see, this definition does not need [preorder A], while op does need this.

Jeremiah Hockaday said:

I first tried to just write notation g:max "ᵒᵖ" => @Dual Aᵒᵈ g but this did not work.

perhaps you can try invoking OrderDual explicitly, like notation g:max "ᵒᵖ" => @Dual (OrderDual _) g

Aaron Liu said:

Jeremiah Hockaday said:

I first tried to just write notation g:max "ᵒᵖ" => @Dual Aᵒᵈ g but this did not work.

perhaps you can try invoking OrderDual explicitly, like notation g:max "ᵒᵖ" => @Dual (OrderDual _) g

Oh sweet, this worked! Thank you. One weird thing is, after I did that the gᵒᵖ notation stopped showing up in the infoview, now it is just g.Dual. Do I need to use Delab to fix this? This is not such a big problem, but it would be nice to fix.
you can try writing a delaborator yourself or you can see if notation3 will do it for you
notation3 did not seem to do anything, what is it supposed to do? I could not find documentation on it.
it's a command defined in mathlib: docs#Mathlib.Notation3.notation3
Ah, I see. I am a bit confused about how to write a delaborator, are there any good resources online that cover this?

So I ended up using something called an "unexpander":

notation:max g:max "ᵒᵖ" => @Dual (OrderDual _) g
open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
@[app_unexpander Dual]
def unexpDual : Unexpander
|`($_ $arg) => `(($arg)ᵒᵖ)
|`($_) => pure <| mkIdent `Dual

It is weaker than a delaborator but it does not require the same monadic language that a delaborator needs. Once I get Peter Selinger hooked on Lean I will make him fix this lol, it works pretty good for now.
This website has a section on unexpanders that I based my code on.
Hi! Sorry for taking so long to respond. I'm unfamiliar with the theory here, so I'll first read the linked papers, and then I'll get back to you.
(I'm nearly done with my schoolwork this semester, after that I'll be free to Lean all summer)
Seems that Definition 4.1 in Peter Selinger's paper is the main notion of games we want to define.

I still insist that instead of getting into the weeds with this QPF stuff, we should define the most general type of games we care about, the "labeled games", and define all other games as subtypes of this. We might have to wait for @Aaron Liu's refactor of QPFs though, since I remember running into universe issues when I last tried this.
Other than that, I think that this material would be nice to have in the main CGT repo.

I noticed that, if recursive functions (sum, MAP, Dual, etc.) are defined using { st } rather than { s | t } proofs become much easier.

Yep, we initially defined games as being made out of two sets, but later we realized the function approach was easier to work with.
As for the dual, it seems to just be the negation operation from standard CGT. Why not write it as -x?

Violeta Hernández said:

As for the dual, it seems to just be the negation operation from standard CGT. Why not write it as -x?

This is a good question, as it functionally is the same definition. One reason not to write the dual as -x is because it is not the additive inverse with respect to sums. This is because of the heterogeneous nature of sums that you noted previously. Another reason to write it as xᵒᵖ is because Peter and I are used to it, but that is much less defensible lol.

Violeta Hernández said:

I still insist that instead of getting into the weeds with this QPF stuff, we should define the most general type of games we care about, the "labeled games", and define all other games as subtypes of this. We might have to wait for Aaron Liu's refactor of QPFs though, since I remember running into universe issues when I last tried this.

I recently proved the following: If G is a polynomial functor and F is a QPF, then G.obj \circ F is a QPF as well. This means that, after showing that G := A \oplus _ is a polynomial functor, I could get the type Primordial A for free using G\circ GameFunctor.

Another thing that I have realized while writing proofs for my type is that normal play games are a subtype of these "Primordial" games: we would say something like : 

def IsNormal {A : Type} {g : Primordial A} : (IsAtom g = false) ∧ ∀ p, ∀ x ∈ moves g p, IsNormal x
termination_by g
decreasing_by Primordial_wf

This gives you the grand unifying theory that you want. How does that sound?

Edit: modified the definition of IsNormal slightly.

The cool thing is that, on the subtype of games that are IsNormal, the sums, negations, and inequalities I have defined are exactly the same as in normal play. (You would have to tweak the definition of sum a bit, but not in a challenging way.)

You could define the normal play games as the games g : Primordial Unit (the singleton type) such that IsNormal g, then the sum would map Primordial Unit -> Primordial Unit -> Primordial (Unit × Unit), and since Unit × Unit ≃ Unit everything would work out.

Edit: I just realized that Empty would be a better choice than Unit, then you could directly prove that \forall g : Primordial Empty, IsNormal g.

Update: I have just pushed a big update, in which I define what it means to be a set coloring game (see IsSC and IsSCP). My coding experience greatly improved after @Violeta Hernández told me not to make Atom A and Comp A into subtypes, and instead prove theorems about games with the hypothesis ha : IsAtom g when I want to look only at atomic games.

In light of this, I have discarded my original plan to make a subtype of set coloring games. Instead, I defined a predicate IsSC on games. This is useful because I often do not need the fact that a game is a set coloring game. I created IsSCP for when i only need some weaker version of IsSC to prove a theorem. After talking with people here, I may define a property IsNormal for when a game is a normal play game. I believe with this we could unify our two theories...

I have just pushed some changes. I added the definition of IsNormal and proved some lemmas about it.
I want to know what lemmas you guys would need from IsNormal in order for it to be of use to you... I figure I can take all of the lemmas I have now and show that an analogous version of them is true for IsNormal games, maybe getting rid of IsAtom wherever necessary (as normal play games necessarily do not have atoms).
